summary: Concrete octagonal light of 1950 on the 95 m cliff at Cap Gaspé, Forillon peninsula, Quebec: third light on the site after the 1873 wooden tower and the 1892 replacement; automated 1972.

structures.type: white octagonal concrete tower with red lantern and gallery
structures.note: built 1949-1950 to Department of Transport plans as part of a coastal modernisation (Quebec inventory); 42 ft per LighthouseFriends

structures.type: wooden combined lighthouse and dwelling, with a square tower rising from the middle of the south face of the dwelling
structures.note: first exhibited 1 November 1892; 46 ft tall; tower collapsed 1946 (Parks Canada; Quebec inventory)

structures.type: square wooden tower with attached keeper's dwelling
structures.note: 30 ft tall; fixed red catoptric light, four lamps, focal plane 350 ft

access.note: In Forillon National Park. Reached on foot or by bicycle, about 4 km from Anse-aux-Amérindiens, along the Les Graves trail; a park entrance fee applies (Parks Canada; LighthouseFriends).

resolved_conflicts.field: tower collapse of the second light
resolved_conflicts.explanation: Parks Canada and the Quebec heritage inventory both give 1946 for the collapse of the second tower. French Wikipedia (lead only, not cited) describes storm damage in 1946. The story says the tower collapsed in 1946, as the two heritage sources do.

resolved_conflicts.field: fire date of the first light
resolved_conflicts.explanation: LighthouseFriends gives 7 November 1890; the Érudit caption and the Quebec inventory give only 1890. The story gives the LighthouseFriends date, marked as LighthouseFriends', and the year from Érudit.
LighthouseFriends spells the first keeper Esnouf in its keeper list and Esmouf in its text; the 1908 annual report prints Le Huquet for Le Huguet. Both variants are noted in the roster.

notes_for_editor: (1) Érudit: only the first page of the article was in the cache. Quotes from it are the opening paragraphs, the 1836 Ferland passage and the 1873/1890 caption. The article's fuller account of the sound signals was not read. The Ferland quotation is second-hand (as Érudit prints it) and is translated in the story. (2) Fire date: 7 November 1890 comes from LighthouseFriends alone. Chronicling America searches for 1890 returned no relevant page, and the corpus Marine reports start in 1900. (3) The 1946 collapse rests on Parks Canada and the Quebec inventory; no newspaper coverage found (one Chronicling America search). (4) Keeper roster: LighthouseFriends' list. The Le Huguet line in the 1908 annual report is OCR'd and matched by position (station and name side by side), so the story says 'probably the same keeper'. (5) Living people: the keepers after about 1960 (Eylmer Langlois, Alf. R. Minchinton) are named only as LighthouseFriends prints them, in role and years, with no personal detail. (6) The wreck of drifter No. 57 is in the Quebec Salvage and Wrecking Company's list, printed in the 1919 Marine report. It places the drifter 'off cape Gaspe', not at the lighthouse. (7) The 1883 fog cannon building and 1950 diaphone shelter are from the Quebec inventory and LighthouseFriends. (8) Access: the Parks Canada page and LighthouseFriends are undated for hours and fees; check the park before a visit. (9) The Coast Guard list footer shows 'Date modified: 2026-07-28' on the Atlantic page. (10) Fact-check 2026-10-27: the 1908 table line ('Cape Gaspe Frs. Le Huquet', printed p. 183, scan p. 192) was checked on the page image; the station and the keeper share a row, and the spelling is as printed. The match to LighthouseFriends' Le Huguet is still a probable identification, not a confirmed one. (11) The Érudit article was read on its first page only; the general statements on fog and beams are marked as general context in the story. (12) The Ferland quotation is second-hand as Érudit prints it; the story says so and marks the translation as ours. (13) The 1901 change to 15-minute fog signals is in the printed report p. 56, which says 'From July 1, 1901'; the OCR for that heading is garbled but the sentence is legible.
